recipe.history:
Tuna is one of the oldest and most widely traveled ingredients in the human culinary story. In Japan, maguro — bluefin tuna — has been central to the sushi and sashimi tradition for centuries, prized for its deep red flesh and clean oceanic richness. The Japanese understood early that tuna demanded restraint: a cold blade, minimal interference, and respect for the raw. Meanwhile, in the Mediterranean, the Romans salted tuna into garum and preserved it in amphoras of oil, trading it across the empire as a staple of everyday sustenance. Sicilian and Spanish fishermen built entire coastal cultures around the mattanza, the seasonal bluefin hunt, where the sea itself seemed to rise and crash with the weight of the catch. The TUNAMI burger takes its name from exactly this duality — the tsunami, that unstoppable wall of ocean force, and the tuna, the creature that lives inside it. It is a pun that earns its place.

Tuna's influence on American food culture arrived in waves — first as canned pantry staple in the early twentieth century, then as sushi-bar sophistication in the 1980s, and finally as a high-low crossover ingredient showing up in everything from poke bowls to competition cookbooks. The bold, assertive umami of tuna — whether raw, seared, or transformed into a sharp aioli — proved to be exactly the kind of flavor that could hold its own against a well-seasoned beef patty. Burger culture in America has always been willing to absorb the world's strongest flavors: kimchi, green chile, foie gras. Tuna fit naturally into that tradition. The salty depth of nori, the clean acidic bite of pickled ginger, the wasabi heat threading through a creamy aioli — these are wave-like flavors, building and crashing, and they belong on a burger the way a good bass line belongs under a melody.

The first time I made this burger, it was late on a Tuesday in October and the kitchen window was fogged from the sear on the cast iron. I was not trying to be clever. I had leftover pickled ginger from a sushi night, a tin of good Italian tuna packed in olive oil, and ground beef that needed to be used. What came out of that improvisation stopped me mid-bite. There was something about the combination — the mineral richness of the beef against the oceanic sharpness of the tuna aioli, the chew of toasted sesame bun against the paper-thin nori — that felt like a memory I hadn't made yet. It reminded me of eating at a diner counter after a long swim in the ocean as a kid, salt-dried and hungry in a way that nothing polite could satisfy. This burger is that hunger made edible.

Cooking the beef patty to medium rare — internal temperature 130 to 135 degrees Fahrenheit, 54 to 57 degrees Celsius — is not a preference. It is the only correct answer. At medium rare, the fat within a well-blended chuck and brisket patty has begun to render and migrate through the meat, basting it from within, while the center retains its moisture and that faint, almost metallic sweetness that disappears entirely once you cross into medium. A burger cooked beyond medium rare is a burger that has surrendered. The crust formed by a hot cast iron or griddle is there to create contrast — the deep Maillard-browned exterior against the yielding, pink, juice-laden interior. That contrast is the whole point. With the TUNAMI in particular, where the toppings carry bold umami and acid, you need a patty that pushes back. Medium rare pushes back. Everything else apologizes.
ingredients: 360g bread flour, plus more for dusting
3 large eggs, room temperature (2 for dough, 1 for egg wash)
1 teaspoon flaky sea salt (for seasoning exterior only)
1 tin (140g) high-quality tuna packed in olive oil, drained
180ml neutral oil (such as grapeseed or light vegetable oil)
1 small garlic clove, microplaned or finely grated
150g fresh young ginger, peeled and sliced paper-thin on a mandoline
4 sheets roasted nori (dried seaweed), cut to roughly fit the patty
Neutral oil or clarified butter (for cooking patties)
instructions: 1. MAKE THE PICKLED GINGER (at least 2 hours ahead, preferably the day before): Toss the sliced ginger with 1 teaspoon salt in a bowl and let it sit for 30 minutes to draw out moisture. Rinse and pat dry. Combine the rice wine vinegar, water, and sugar in a small saucepan over medium heat and stir until the sugar dissolves. Do not boil. Pour the warm brine over the ginger in a clean jar or bowl, press the ginger down so it is submerged, and let cool to room temperature. Refrigerate for at least 2 hours. The ginger will keep for up to 3 weeks refrigerated.

2. MAKE THE BRIOCHE BUNS — DOUGH: Combine the warm milk, warm water, and yeast in the bowl of a stand mixer fitted with the dough hook. Let bloom for 5 minutes until foamy. Add the sugar, salt, 2 eggs, and all the flour. Mix on low speed until the dough comes together, about 3 minutes. Increase to medium and knead for 5 minutes until smooth.

3. ENRICH THE DOUGH: With the mixer running on medium-low, add the softened butter one or two cubes at a time, waiting for each addition to incorporate before adding the next. This process will take 8–10 minutes. The finished dough should be soft, glossy, and pull away cleanly from the bowl sides. If it is too sticky after all butter is added, knead 2–3 minutes more.

4. FIRST RISE: Transfer the dough to a lightly oiled bowl, cover tightly with plastic wrap, and let rise at room temperature until doubled in size, approximately 1.5 to 2 hours. Alternatively, refrigerate overnight for a slow rise and richer flavor.

5. SHAPE THE BUNS: Punch down the dough and turn it onto a lightly floured surface. Divide into 4 equal portions (roughly 180g each). Shape each into a tight ball by pulling the surface taut and pinching the seam underneath. Place on a parchment-lined baking sheet, spaced well apart. Gently flatten each ball with your palm to about 2.5cm thickness.

6. SECOND RISE: Cover the shaped buns loosely with plastic wrap or a damp towel and let rise until puffed and nearly doubled, about 45 minutes to 1 hour. Preheat your oven to 190°C / 375°F during the last 20 minutes of this rise.

7. BAKE THE BUNS: Beat the remaining egg with 1 tablespoon of water to make an egg wash. Brush the tops of the buns gently with egg wash and sprinkle with sesame seeds. Bake for 16–19 minutes until deep golden brown. Transfer to a wire rack and cool completely before slicing — at least 30 minutes.

8. MAKE THE TUNA AIOLI: Place the egg yolks, Dijon mustard, garlic, rice wine vinegar, and a pinch of salt in a medium bowl (or the jar of an immersion blender). Whisk or blend to combine. Very slowly — drop by drop at first — drizzle in the neutral oil while whisking vigorously or blending continuously. Once the emulsion is established and the aioli begins to thicken, you can add the oil in a thin, steady stream. Whisk in the olive oil at the end.

9. FINISH THE TUNA AIOLI: Fold in the drained tuna, soy sauce, sesame oil, and wasabi paste. Use a fork to break the tuna into the aioli, leaving some texture — you want it spreadable but not completely smooth. Taste and adjust wasabi, salt, and vinegar. Cover and refrigerate until needed.

10. BLEND AND FORM THE PATTIES: Combine the ground chuck and ground brisket in a large bowl. Use your hands to gently mix the two cuts together — do not overwork the meat, which toughens it. Divide into 4 equal portions (approximately 168g each). Shape each into a patty roughly 1.5cm wider than your bun (it will shrink). Press a shallow dimple into the center of each patty with your thumb to prevent doming during cooking. Refrigerate on a plate, uncovered, for at least 20 minutes.

11. SEASON AND COOK THE PATTIES: Remove the patties from the refrigerator 10 minutes before cooking. Season both sides generously with flaky sea salt and coarsely ground black pepper immediately before cooking — not in advance, as salt draws out moisture. Heat a cast iron skillet or heavy griddle over high heat until smoking. Add a thin film of neutral oil or clarified butter. Place the patties in the pan without crowding. Cook undisturbed for 2.5 to 3 minutes until a deep brown crust has formed on the underside.

12. FLIP AND FINISH TO MEDIUM RARE: Flip each patty once. Cook for an additional 2 to 2.5 minutes. Check the internal temperature with an instant-read thermometer inserted through the side into the center of the patty — you are targeting 130–135°F (54–57°C) for medium rare. Remove the patties from the pan and let them rest on a wire rack for 3–4 minutes. Do not press them. Do not skip the rest.

13. TOAST THE BUNS: While the patties rest, reduce the skillet heat to medium. Add the 2 tablespoons of unsalted butter to the same pan and let it foam. Place the buns cut-side down and toast until golden and caramelized, 60–90 seconds. Remove and set aside.

14. PREPARE THE NORI: Lay the nori sheets flat. If using full sheets, cut each to roughly the diameter of your patty using scissors. Toast briefly over the residual heat of the burner for 5 seconds per side if they feel soft, until they are crisp and fragrant.

15. ASSEMBLE THE TUNAMI BURGER: Spread a generous layer of tuna aioli on both the cut top and bottom bun. Place a butter lettuce leaf on the bottom bun. Lay a sheet of toasted nori directly on the lettuce. Set the rested patty on the nori. Fan 3–4 slices of avocado over the patty. Pile a small tangle of drained pickled ginger on top of the avocado. Sprinkle with black sesame seeds. Crown with the top bun. Serve immediately.
